lesson.title: Making + Mean Something New
lesson.summary: Operator overloading lets you redefine what +, -, ==, and other built-in operators do when applied to objects of a class you write, by implementing the matching dunder method.
lesson.body:
In earlier chapters you have used + to add numbers and to concatenate strings, and you may have noticed it behaves differently depending on what it is applied to: 2 + 3 gives 5, but "a" + "b" gives "ab". That is not a coincidence and it is not two unrelated features that both happen to be called +. Both are the same operator, routed to two different dunder methods depending on the type of the left operand: int.__add__ in one case, str.__add__ in the other. Operator overloading is the general name for this pattern: the same symbol behaves differently depending on which dunder method the type on the left provides. It is called overloading because one symbol is doing more than one job, and which job it does depends on the operand's type.

When you write a class of your own, you can plug into this same system. Python does not let you invent new operators (you cannot make up a symbol like <> and give it meaning), but it does let you define what the existing operators do for instances of your class, by implementing the dunder method that operator is wired to.

```python
class Vector:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __add__(self, other):
        return Vector(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y)

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Vector({self.x}, {self.y})"

v1 = Vector(1, 2)
v2 = Vector(3, 4)
print(v1 + v2)
```

This prints Vector(4, 6). Writing v1 + v2 causes Python to call v1.__add__(v2), which returns a brand new Vector built from the sum of each coordinate: 1 + 3 for x, and 2 + 4 for y.

It is worth being precise about why this is useful, rather than just a syntax trick. Without __add__, combining two vectors would require a method with a name you invent, like v1.add(v2) or combine(v1, v2), and every piece of code using Vector would need to know that specific name. By overloading +, Vector objects can be combined using the exact same syntax that already means "combine these two things" everywhere else in Python. Code that works with vectors ends up reading the way the math it represents reads, which is the entire point: operator overloading exists to make your objects fit naturally into the language, not to make code shorter for its own sake.

The table of operators to dunder methods is long, and you will meet several of the most common ones over the next few chapters: __eq__ for ==, __lt__ for <, __add__ for +, and __mul__ for *, among others. All of them follow the pattern shown here: define the method, and the operator starts calling it automatically for objects of your class.
